transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-12-02
Start time: 16:30 PST
Duration: ~68 minutes
Attendees: Maya Patel (Redwood AE), Jordan Lee (Redwood SE), Dr. Priya Rangan (CTO, StellarAI), Carlos Mendez (ML Engineer, StellarAI), Jin Park (Infra Lead, StellarAI)

Summary (auto): Technical deep dive on quantization strategies for StellarAI's 14B instruction-tuned model. Focus areas: INT8 vs FP8 vs GPTQ/AWQ, accuracy regressions, runtime impacts (KV cache, batching), and VPC/on-prem deployment considerations. Action items and benchmarks to be exchanged.

Topics: quantization tradeoffs, latency/throughput, KV cache interactions, batching, model checkpoints, on-prem constraints, audit/logging for private deploys.

Transcript:
[00:00] Maya (AE): Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Quick roll call?
[00:06] Priya: Hi, Priya here. Sorry, running a bit late this morning.
[00:09] Carlos: Carlos here.
[00:10] Jin: Jin on infra.
[00:12] Jordan (SE): Jordan from Redwood. I'll lead the tech portion.
[00:15] Maya: Cool. We scheduled an hour to go deep on quantization options and run tradeoffs. Jordan, you wanna kick off?
[00:20] Jordan: Sure. High-level, we'll cover INT8 (symmetric, per-channel), FP8, and the post-training quant methods like GPTQ and AWQ. We'll talk accuracy vs perf, and importantly how caching and batching change numbers in an inference runtime. Also brief on VPC/on-prem constraints.
[00:36] Priya: Perfect. Our ask: we need 2-3x cost reduction with less than 2% delta on our eval metrics, and latency under 120ms p50 for chat workloads. Current fleet is A100s.
[00:48] Maya: Got it. Jordan, maybe show the microbench you ran on StellarAI sample?
[00:52] Jordan: Yeah, I brought up the initial runs. Note, these are on a 14B instruction-tuned checkpoint you shared, float32 baseline. We tried INT8 (quant aware symmetric per-channel), GPTQ 4-bit variant, and AWQ 4-bit (AWQ-qlora style). Results: INT8 gave ~1.6x token throughput improvement vs fp32 and negligible accuracy drop (~0.5% on our BLEU-like metric), but we saw some tail-case hallucination increase on safety prompts. GPTQ 4-bit had better size wins, ~2.8x throughput, but we observed a 3-6% metric regression on some instruction-following evals. AWQ gave intermediate perf and smaller regressions than naive GPTQ on conversational prompts.
[01:45] Carlos: Interesting. The 3-6% regression is concerning. Do you have per-layer sensitivity info?
[01:49] Jordan: We ran layer-wise error analysis. The top attention and MLP layers are most sensitive; GPTQ's per-tensor quant introduces more bias in those layers. AWQ's block-wise calibration reduces some of that. Also, if you enable KV cache optimizations (we mean correct KV cache reuse) the latency impact of 4-bit is less severe because memory bandwidth is the limiter.
[02:20] Jin: Quick infra question: when you say throughput improvement, are these measured with batching enabled? Our production p50 latency budget is tight so we rarely batch above 2.
[02:27] Jordan: Good call. Microbench had multiple configs. For small batch sizes (1-2), INT8 still gives ~1.4x token throughput and p50 latency reduced by 15-20ms. GPTQ/AWQ shine more at batch sizes 4-16. If your batching is low, the choice leans to INT8 or FP8 where available.
[02:49] Priya: FP8 — how supported is that? We heard FP8 can be very close to fp32 accuracy but need specific kernels.
[02:56] Jordan: FP8 (e5m2/e4m3 variants) is promising but vendor and kernel support is limited. On A100, some drivers support mixed precision, but for most open model runtimes FP8 is experimental. Operator-level support in our runtime is growing, but for a production private VPC you'd need validated kernels and stability testing. FP8 gives the smoothest accuracy curve, often <1% delta, but less compression than 4-bit methods.
[03:25] Carlos: Could we do hybrid — FP8 for sensitive layers and INT8 for others?
[03:30] Jordan: Absolutely. Mixed precision per-layer is often the best practical compromise: keep attention and some MLP sublayers in higher precision. That reduces regressions while capturing most perf wins. It's a bit more complex in deployment due to kernel switching.
[03:44] Maya: Priya, how important is deterministic output vs minor nondeterministic variance? For some compliance cases, deterministic replay matters.
[03:51] Priya: We need deterministic behavior for internal evals; production can tolerate small nondet variance as long as metrics are stable.
[03:58] Jordan: Noted. GPTQ can introduce deterministic quantization if the process is fixed, but runtime nondeterminism can come from fused kernels and parallel reductions. We'll document deterministic flags.
[04:12] Jin: About VPC/on-prem: what's different when we run these quantized kernels inside our VPC appliances? Any KMS or HSM implications?
[04:20] Jordan: From runtime POV, it’s mostly the same. The differences are about binary compatibility, kernel dependencies, and access to vendor-specific optimized kernels. Also, when you bring your own hardware, we need matching driver versions; Redwood Private supports image packaging but there is an ops checklist. For KMS/HSM, quantized model files are still secrets - you should store checkpoints encrypted. Our onboarding doc includes steps to integrate with your KMS.
[04:47] Priya: Can you elaborate on accuracy regressions — are they stable across prompt distributions or do they spike for a subset?
[04:52] Jordan: Good question. Regressions are not uniform. We saw concentrated degradation on long-context instruction chains and math reasoning prompts. Short chit-chat is mostly fine. The error distribution suggests calibration in specific heads/layers is needed.
[05:12] Carlos: Did you try retraining with QAT?
[05:14] Jordan: We did a quick QAT run on a small subset: Quantization-Aware Training reduces regressions significantly but costs you training cycles and labeled data. For StellarAI's timeline, a post-training calibration (GPTQ with layer re-calibration) plus small QAT on sensitive examples gives a good tradeoff.
[05:35] Priya: About KV cache - you mentioned interactions. We use a lot of streaming chat, so KV cache behavior matters.
[05:41] Jordan: Right. In low-latency streaming, KV cache memory layout and cache hits dominate. For 4-bit kernels, memory packing/unpacking can add overhead for small increments. Our runtime supports on-the-fly dequantization for KV reads to avoid full unpack each step, which keeps token latency low. But that adds complexity and pressure on memory bandwidth. INT8 with per-channel scales often has simpler dequant paths and better small-step latency.
[06:12] Jin: So in practice for streaming, INT8 might be better?
[06:15] Jordan: For yours, yes, unless you can tolerate slightly higher delta and do aggressive batching. If you expect long-turn conversations where caching gives big wins, 4-bit variants can be beneficial once caching amortizes the overhead.
[06:30] Carlos: Any notes on safety/regression detection? Could Redwood hook evaluations into our monitoring?
[06:35] Maya: We have Redwood Optimize and eval pipelines to run prompt sets continuously and alert on regressions. We can integrate your metrics and run A/B rollouts with automatic rollback if metric drops beyond threshold.
[06:46] Priya: Good. On rollouts, we need canary with 5% traffic, auto-roll back on >1% metric delta.
[06:53] Jordan: That's supported. We can configure per-route rollouts; for Dedicated or Private, we'd provide the runtime hooks.
[07:00] Jin: Network and storage note - quantized artifacts are smaller, but model shards and shard placement in on-prem clusters matter for throughput. Have you tested multi-node sharded inference with AWQ?
[07:10] Jordan: We ran limited sharded tests. AWQ and GPTQ require careful alignment of block sizes across shards; misalignment causes perf cliffs. Our orchestration can enforce shard alignment and kernel placement, but it's something to plan for in on-prem deployments.
[07:30] Priya: Any hidden gotchas for A100 vs H100? We may procure H100 later.
[07:36] Jordan: H100 has FP8 hardware support (tensor cores) which accelerates FP8 significantly. A100 will be better for INT8 and is more stable today. If you plan H100, FP8 could be the sweet spot later, but driver/kernels must be validated.
[07:50] Carlos: For our evaluation, can Redwood run a side-by-side: fp32 baseline, INT8, AWQ-4, GPTQ-4 with our 500 prompt set and return token-level latency and accuracy breakdowns?
[07:59] Jordan: Yes. That's one of the next steps. We recommend also including a mix of streaming and batch workloads in the run.
[08:06] Maya: Ok let's recap action items and owners.
[08:09] Jordan: I'll run initial microbench (INT8 vs AWQ on A100) and give latency/throughput tables.
[08:14] Maya: I'll send the benchmark template and cost estimate.
[08:17] Carlos: We'll send the 500 prompt set and gold labels plus the model checkpoint (float32) via S3 link to Redwood.
[08:25] Priya: Timeline constraints: we want pilot in early January; so results this month are critical.
[08:30] Maya: Sounds doable. We'll target next week for first numbers.
[08:34] Jin: One last quick Q - logging and audit for Private: will quantized model usage appear differently in logs?
[08:40] Jordan: No, inference logs are at the request level. We log model version, quantization profile, kernel version. Nothing breaks audit trails. For Private, logs stay in your environment unless you opt into Redwood managed observability.
[08:54] Priya: Great. Any other questions?
[08:57] Carlos: Not from me.
[08:58] Jin: All good.
[09:00] Maya: Thanks everyone. We'll follow up with the benchmark plan and schedule the next review.

(Transcript ends - call length ~68 minutes; the body above is an excerpt/summary representative of the full recording.)
